title: fix(driver-sql): refuse an unbacked upsert conflict target on MySQL before compiling
body:
Fixes #8621

Auto-adjudicated to **Option A** — a pre-flight refusal in `driver-sql` — on sibling-branch inheritance from #8445 (SQLite) and #8567 / #8413 (Postgres). Option B (document the divergence) was rejected. No fork-back was triggered: no MySQL-specific semantic difference blocked the mother ruling. One condition the ruling does not reach is filed separately as #8755, not silently re-decided (see "Scope boundary").

## The mechanism, because it could not be the existing one

The refusal already in the tree is **reactive**: `sql-driver.ts` catches a server error via `isUnbackedConflictTargetError` and rethrows `refuseUnbackedConflictTarget`. On SQLite and Postgres the server does raise — `ON CONFLICT (email)` names an arbiter index, the planner cannot find one, and the statement is refused before it writes.

On MySQL no error is ever raised, because the conflict target never reaches the server. knex compiles the driver's exact call to `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, which takes no target at all — pinned with no server needed:

```
knex('t').insert({...}).onConflict(['email']).merge(['title']).toSQL()
  mysql2 -> insert into `t` (…) values (?, ?, ?)
            on duplicate key update `title` = values(`title`)     ← no `email`
```

So `upsert` now consults the table's **physical** PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE indexes before compiling, via the existing `introspectIndexes`. What is reused is the **answer** — the same `refuseUnbackedConflictTarget` wording, `code` and `status`, per #5240 (one condition, one wording). What could not be reused is the code path.

### Why MySQL only

Not a dialect exemption — the opposite. SQLite and Postgres already refuse this call with this sentence, and they attach the **server's own text** as `cause`, which is the ground truth an operator debugging the table wants and which no pre-flight can reconstruct. Running the pre-flight there would replace a planner verdict with an introspection verdict and discard that `cause`, on the two dialects that are already correct. The criterion is "the compiler drops the conflict target, so the server can never be asked".

The reverse verification measures exactly that asymmetry (below).

### Why it refuses only what it can prove

A false refusal breaks a working merge — the expensive direction. Every uncertain answer proceeds: a failed introspection, a table reporting **no keys at all** (indistinguishable from a table that does not exist, since MySQL's `information_schema` answers zero rows either way), and a possibly stale cache, which is re-read from the database before any refusal is thrown. The pre-flight also runs only when the caller **names** a target — the default `['id']` is this driver's own primary key on every table it creates — and it runs before `fillAutoNumberFields`, so a refused call never burns an autonumber reservation.

## What was measured, on real servers

A live **MySQL 8.0.46** was raised in this container (Ubuntu noble `mysql-server`, `mysqld --daemonize`, `default_time_zone='+08:00'`) and a live **Postgres 16.13** (`initdb` + `pg_ctl`, `timezone=Asia/Shanghai`), so all three cells of the dialect matrix ran here rather than riding on CI.

**Before**, against `main` — #8592's transcript reproduced line for line:

```
seed  upsert({email:'a@b.com',     tax_id:'T-1', title:'first'},  ['email'])  -> resolved
B     upsert({email:'other@b.com', tax_id:'T-1', title:'second'}, ['email'])  -> resolved
        ONE row: merged on `tax_id`, which the caller never named.
D     seed, then upsert({email:'a@b.com', tax_id:'T-2'}, ['email'])           -> resolved
        TWO rows, both email='a@b.com': the requested merge did not happen either.
```

**After**: both calls are `VALIDATION_ERROR` / 400, with the same first sentence SQLite and Postgres produce, and **nothing is written** — the table is empty afterwards, which is the assertion that separates a pre-flight from a post-hoc classification.

Controls, all on the same live MySQL: a target a UNIQUE index does back still merges; the primary key named explicitly is accepted; the default no-`conflictKeys` path is untouched. On SQLite and live Postgres the whole sweep is unchanged, `cause` included.

## Pins: rewritten to the refusal, not relaxed

#8592 wrote its MySQL section as characterization and said the pins would go red when this card landed and must then be **rewritten to the refusal**. That is what this PR does. `code` and `status` are both asserted; the shared-wording pin asserts the identical sentence the SQLite/Postgres sweep asserts.

⚠️ **One thing to review deliberately: #8622's identity pin moved fixtures.** It pins identity preservation *across a merge on a key the caller never named*, and on the mismatched table that call is now refused — the phenomenon it measures no longer occurs there, so the pin could not stay put. Its assertion, strength and failure message are **untouched**; only the table changed, to one where a wrong-key merge still happens after this card (both columns unique — #8755). Deleting it, or relaxing it to fit the refusal, would have dropped #8622's only MySQL-cell coverage of a landed fix. Its docblock records that #8621's container executed it on live MySQL for the first time, green, and keeps its standing instruction intact.

`sql-driver-sys-setting-organization-unique.test.ts` (#8629's pin) was not touched.

## Reverse verification — direction predicted before running

Predicted, with the fix committed first and then the call site's `this.isMysql` guard inverted to `!this.isMysql`: the MySQL pins go red, **and** the SQLite/Postgres sweep goes red *differently* — its refusal pins stay green (same wording, code and status) while its `cause` pin fails, because the pre-flight answers first and its cause is the driver's introspection sentence, not the server's `insert into … on conflict …`.

Measured; it matched exactly: **7 failures — 5 MySQL pins, plus the one `cause` pin on each of SQLite and Postgres.** The fix was restored with `git checkout HEAD -- …` (never `git stash`).

## Scope boundary — filed, not smuggled in

`ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` carries no conflict target **even when the named one is backed**, so a second unique index can still absorb the conflict on MySQL. Measured here with both business columns unique:

```
seed  upsert({email:'a@b.com',     tax_id:'T-1'}, ['email'])  -> seeded
B     upsert({email:'other@b.com', tax_id:'T-1'}, ['email'])  -> ONE row, merged on tax_id
```

That is a different condition with a different fix and a genuinely wider accept-set question, so it is filed as **#8755** and pinned here as the boundary — nobody should read this PR as making MySQL honour `conflictKeys` as a target. #8755 is not addressed here.

| `check:type-check-debt` (`--re-measure`, full closure built) | 0 |

Re-derived against the actual changed paths with `scripts/pm/dispatch-gates.mjs`; it named exactly the families the dispatch listed, no additions.

Tests, on the merged tree with all three dialects live:

- `@objectstack/driver-sql` — **100 files, 2096 tests, all passing** (SQLite + live PG 16.13 + live MySQL 8.0.46, `TZ=America/New_York`; no cell skipped)
- `@objectstack/driver-turso` — 37 files, 986 tests (the direct `SqlDriver` subclass)
- `@objectstack/objectql` — 206 files, 3629 tests (the one production caller passing `conflictKeys`)
- `pnpm --filter @objectstack/driver-sql typecheck` — clean
- `pnpm --filter @objectstack/spec check:generated` after merging `main` — all 13 artifacts up to date

Changeset: `driver-sql` **minor**, stating plainly that MySQL calls which previously "resolved" now throw.
